title: 900 metres of granite: the story of El Capitan
summary: El Capitan rises about 900 metres from the floor of Yosemite Valley as one unbroken wall of granite.
body: El Capitan rises about 900 metres from the floor of Yosemite Valley in California. It is a single wall of granite, and from the valley it looks less like a mountain than a vertical cliff.

The valley itself was carved by glaciers. Over a very long time, moving ice ground down the landscape, leaving steep walls on either side and a wide, flat floor. El Capitan is one of the walls that was left standing.
That history is why the view is so striking. Because the granite is one unbroken face rather than a series of ledges and slopes, the eye has very little to rest on until it reaches the top.
If you are photographing it, look for something in the foreground, such as trees or the valley floor, to give the scale some context. On its own, a bare wall of rock can be hard to read.

title: Why Scotland’s Highlands were once joined to America
summary: The Scottish Highlands and North America's Appalachians were once part of one mountain chain, split apart when the Atlantic opened.
body: The Scottish Highlands and the Appalachian Mountains of North America look like they belong to different worlds. One is a rugged corner of northern Britain, the other a long range running down the eastern side of North America.
Yet they were once part of the same mountain chain. The two sit on opposite sides of an ocean today, but that ocean has not always been there.

They were separated when the Atlantic Ocean opened. As the ocean widened, the land on either side moved apart, and the old chain was split in two, with one part ending up in Scotland and the other in North America.
It is a good reminder that mountains are not fixed features. Next time you are walking in the Highlands, you are standing on the remains of a range that once stretched across what is now open sea.

title: The puffin’s beak glows under UV light. Here’s why
summary: Under ultraviolet light a puffin's beak fluoresces, a glow that other puffins can probably see even though we cannot.
body: Puffins are sometimes nicknamed sea parrots, and it is easy to see why. Their bright, chunky beaks are among the most recognisable in the bird world.
In 2018 it was reported that there is more to those beaks than meets the eye. Under ultraviolet light, a puffin's beak fluoresces, giving off a glow.
We cannot see that glow with our own eyes. Birds, however, can see ultraviolet light, and humans cannot. That means the effect is visible to other puffins, even though it is hidden from us.

Why might it matter? The glow may play a role in signalling between birds, although it is worth being careful here. Seeing that something glows is not the same as knowing what it is for, and the full purpose is still open to question.

title: The largest living structure on Earth, explained
summary: The Great Barrier Reef, off Australia, is over 2,300 km long and built entirely by tiny animals called coral polyps.
body: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest living structure on Earth. It lies off the coast of Australia and stretches for more than 2,300 km.
It is easy to think of a reef as a kind of rock or underwater landscape, but it is something different. The reef is built by tiny animals called coral polyps.
Each polyp is small, but together they add up. Over time, huge numbers of them build the structure that makes up the reef, which is why it counts as a living thing rather than simply a place.
That is also why a reef needs care. Because it is made of living animals, it can be affected by changes in its surroundings, and it is not something that can simply be left to look after itself.

title: How the Arctic fox changes its coat with the seasons
summary: Arctic foxes turn white for winter and brown-grey for summer, a coat that works as camouflage and insulation.
body: The Arctic fox has one of the most useful wardrobes in the animal world. It changes its coat with the seasons, turning white for winter and brown-grey for summer.

The change is a form of camouflage. A white fox is hard to spot against snow, and a brown-grey one blends in with the ground once the snow has gone. The result is that the fox is disguised all year round.
The coat does a second job as well. Arctic foxes live in very cold places, and their fur keeps them warm in temperatures down to about −50°C.

Put together, it is a neat piece of design. The same fur that hides the fox from view also protects it from some of the harshest conditions on the planet. It is a good example of how an animal can be suited to its surroundings in more than one way.

title: Mount Fuji: the postcard that is still an active volcano
summary: Japan's highest peak at 3,776 m, Mount Fuji is an active volcano that last erupted in 1707.
body: Mount Fuji is one of the most photographed mountains in the world. Its smooth, symmetrical shape has made it a familiar image on postcards and in paintings.

It is also Japan's highest peak, at 3,776 m. From a distance it looks calm and settled, which makes it easy to forget what it actually is. The shape is so regular that it can seem almost too perfect to be real.
Mount Fuji is an active volcano. It last erupted in 1707, which is a long time ago by human standards but not very long at all for a volcano.

That does not make the scenery any less beautiful, but it does add something to the view. The mountain that looks so peaceful in a photograph is a living part of the landscape, and it is worth seeing it that way.

title: Why a tiger’s stripes go skin deep
summary: A tiger's stripes are on its skin as well as its fur, and no two tigers share the same pattern.
body: A tiger's stripes are one of the most famous patterns in nature, and they run deeper than you might expect. The pattern is on the tiger's skin as well as in its fur.

That means the stripes are not just a surface effect. If a tiger's fur were removed, the markings would still be there on the skin beneath. The stripes are part of the animal itself, not just a coat that sits on top.
Each pattern is also unique. No two tigers have the same one, which makes stripes a kind of fingerprint. Even tigers born to the same mother have patterns that are their own.

This is useful for anyone who studies or photographs tigers, because the stripes can be used to identify individual animals. Two photographs taken in different places can show that it is the same tiger, simply by comparing the markings.

title: The owl that hunts in daylight
summary: Unlike most owls, snowy owls are active by day, which suits an Arctic summer when the sun does not set.
body: When you picture an owl, you probably picture it at night. The snowy owl does not fit that image. Unlike most owls, it is active by day.
There is a practical reason for it. In the Arctic summer the sun does not set, so there is no real night to hunt in. An owl that waited for darkness would be waiting a long time.
The snowy owl is built for the cold as well. Its feet are feathered right down to the toes, which helps to protect them in the kind of conditions it lives in.
For photographers, a daytime owl is a gift. You do not have to work in the dark, and the bird is often easier to see against pale surroundings than a night-time species would be.

title: Five ways to get sharper wildlife photos
summary: Five practical habits, from shutter speed to patience, that will help you get sharper wildlife photographs.
body: First, use a fast shutter speed. For moving animals, 1/1000 s or faster is a sensible starting point. Slower speeds are the most common reason that a photo of a moving animal looks soft.

Second, use continuous autofocus so the camera keeps tracking the animal as it moves. Shoot at the animal's eye level where you can, and focus on the eye. A sharp eye makes the whole picture feel sharp.

Third, make use of early or late light. It is softer and more flattering, and it often gives you more to work with than the harsh light of midday. Soft light also helps to show the detail in fur and feathers.
Finally, keep your distance and be patient. Staying back protects the animal and often gets you more natural behaviour. Wait, watch, and let the moment come to you.
